profiles.name: Richard Aurandt
profiles.excerpt: Richard Aurandt was one of Hollywood radio's busiest dramatic composers and conductors, shaping the sound of Philip Marlowe, Rocky Jordan, Wild Bill Hickok and other West Coast series.
profiles.bio_html:
Richard Aurandt belonged to the generation of radio musicians who learned to write quickly, conduct cleanly and make a small orchestra carry the emotional weight of an entire scene. A 1944 Radio Life profile described him as a conductor, composer and arranger with musical experience stretching back to childhood, when he worked as a pianist and organist while also pursuing technical interests outside music.

By the late 1940s Aurandt had become one of the dependable musical architects of Hollywood radio drama. He supplied the music for the CBS Adventures of Philip Marlowe, where the score had to support Gerald Mohr's hard-boiled narration without overwhelming it, and he also worked on Rocky Jordan, Voyage of the Scarlet Queen, Jeff Regan, Investigator and Wild Bill Hickok. Contemporary scripts credit his special music as conceived and conducted by Aurandt, a useful reminder that radio scoring was often composed for the specific dramatic rhythm of a weekly broadcast rather than drawn from a stock library.

Golden Radio Hour's broader people index currently connects Aurandt to hundreds of preserved music credits: 177 on Wild Bill Hickok, 140 on Rocky Jordan, 94 on Philip Marlowe, 33 on Voyage of the Scarlet Queen and 28 on Jeff Regan. Those are composer, conductor, music and organ credits, not a dozen acting performances.

profiles.name: Milton Charles
profiles.excerpt: Milton Charles carried the improvisational craft of silent-film organ playing into decades of radio, scoring soap operas, westerns and dramatic programs almost in real time.
profiles.bio_html:
Milton Charles learned accompaniment when a musician still had to create a film score live in the theatre. Born in San Jose in 1897, he studied piano as a child, became a church organist at thirteen and was soon playing major silent-film houses. That work demanded instant judgment about mood, character and pacing, skills that transferred naturally to radio when sound films reduced the market for theatre organists.

Charles moved into broadcasting and became one of the medium's working organ specialists. He later recalled racing between studios to score several daytime serials in succession, often receiving the story only shortly before airtime. His radio work included Amos 'n' Andy, Ma Perkins, The Road of Life, Roy Rogers and Gene Autry programs, and he served as a CBS staff musician. The organ could supply suspense, romance, transition and continuity with a flexibility that made it indispensable to live radio.

Golden Radio Hour's broader people index currently preserves 54 music credits for Roy Rogers, 20 for Rocky Jordan, nine for Jeff Regan, Investigator, eight for A Man Called X and additional music credits elsewhere. His record belongs with radio musicians, not in an actor queue.

profiles.name: Cy Feuer
profiles.excerpt: Before Cy Feuer became a legendary Broadway producer, he was a Juilliard-trained trumpeter, studio music director and radio composer whose work included Escape and Casey, Crime Photographer.
profiles.bio_html:
Cy Feuer is remembered primarily as the Broadway producer behind Guys and Dolls, Can-Can and How to Succeed in Business Without Really Trying, but that later career grew from serious musical training. Born Seymour Arnold Feuerman in Brooklyn in 1911, he played trumpet professionally as a teenager, studied at Juilliard, worked in theatre orchestras and eventually became a composer and music-department head at Republic Pictures.

Radio was part of the transition between his work as a musician and his later identity as a producer. GRH's detailed people data credits Feuer with composing, conducting or providing music on 42 preserved Escape broadcasts, along with music work on Casey, Crime Photographer and Columbia Workshop. His radio scoring belongs to the same practical show-business education that later let him evaluate songs, orchestration and dramatic pacing on Broadway.

After returning to New York in 1947, Feuer partnered with Ernest Martin and became one of the dominant musical-theatre producers of the postwar era. For GRH, the important correction is chronological: the Broadway legend did not suddenly appear as a producer. He arrived there after years spent as a working musician, arranger, composer and music director in film and radio.

profiles.name: Jerry Goldsmith
profiles.excerpt: Jerry Goldsmith learned screen scoring under live-radio pressure at CBS, writing music week after week before becoming one of the most influential film composers of his generation.
profiles.bio_html:
Jerry Goldsmith's celebrated film career began inside broadcasting. Born in Los Angeles in 1929, he studied piano, composition and counterpoint and took film-composition classes with Miklós Rózsa. At twenty-one he entered CBS not as a featured composer but as a clerk-typist. Writing music for an employee program helped open the door to professional assignments on live radio and television.

Radio forced Goldsmith to become fast, flexible and dramatically precise. He wrote scores for programs such as Romance and CBS Radio Workshop, and GRH's detailed people data preserves 47 Frontier Gentleman composer/conductor credits, six CBS Radio Workshop music credits and a Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar music-supervisor credit. The weekly production cycle taught him to find a musical idea quickly and make it serve story rather than call attention to itself.

Goldsmith carried that discipline into television and then film, eventually scoring works including Planet of the Apes, Patton, Chinatown, Alien and The Omen. GRH therefore treats his radio credits as the beginning of the mature composer, not as miscellaneous early appearances mistakenly filed under performer.

profiles.name: Anton Karas
profiles.excerpt: Anton Karas made the zither the unmistakable sound of Harry Lime, carrying the musical identity of The Third Man directly into Orson Welles's radio adventures.
profiles.bio_html:
Anton Karas was a Viennese zither player whose life changed when director Carol Reed heard him performing in Vienna and chose his instrument as the musical voice of The Third Man. Born in 1906, Karas transformed an instrument many international listeners barely knew into one of the most recognizable sounds in postwar popular culture. His recording of the film's theme became a worldwide hit.

When Orson Welles returned to the character Harry Lime for radio in The Lives of Harry Lime, the zither sound came with him. Karas's music was not simply decorative. It instantly re-established the sly, cosmopolitan world audiences associated with Lime and allowed the radio series to inherit part of the film's identity before Welles spoke a line.

Golden Radio Hour currently indexes 52 preserved Lives of Harry Lime programs under Karas in the performer index, while the detailed people data records 104 zither/performer credits. Those entries should be understood as musical participation and theme identity, not as acting roles.

profiles.name: Rex Koury
profiles.excerpt: Rex Koury carried theatre-organ instincts into radio scoring and wrote the western theme that became inseparable from Gunsmoke in both radio and television.
profiles.bio_html:
Rex Koury began with the theatre organ. Born in London in 1911 and brought to the United States as a child, he became fascinated by pipe-organ accompaniment to silent films and was working professionally while still young. As silent-film accompaniment declined, he moved through orchestras, studios and radio, where the ability to create atmosphere quickly remained valuable.

Koury's defining radio work was Gunsmoke. He composed the theme, conducted the radio orchestra and wrote much of the interior music that gave Dodge City its musical atmosphere. Koury later recalled developing the internal scoring before settling on the theme itself. His western melody survived the transition to television, giving the franchise a musical continuity even when the cast and medium changed.

Golden Radio Hour's broader people index currently preserves 416 Gunsmoke composer, conductor, music and performer-tagged credits for Koury, plus smaller organ and music credits on other programs. That scale makes clear why a generic performer label badly understates his place in the archive.

profiles.name: Norman Luboff
profiles.excerpt: Norman Luboff used The Railroad Hour as a national laboratory for choral storytelling before building one of America's best-known professional choirs.
profiles.bio_html:
Norman Luboff's career joined serious choral training to the commercial demands of American broadcasting. Born in Chicago in 1917, he studied piano and voice, attended the University of Chicago and Central College, and pursued graduate work with composer Leo Sowerby. He supported his musical development by singing and arranging for radio, then served in the Army Signal Corps during World War II.

After radio work in New York, Luboff moved to Hollywood to become choral director of The Railroad Hour. The chorus was not treated as a decorative extra. Contemporary program material described it as part of the dramatic machinery, establishing mood, emphasizing action and connecting the narrative around Gordon MacRae and the guest stars. GRH's detailed people data currently preserves 429 Railroad Hour credits spanning choral direction, composition, conducting, direction and performance tagging.

Luboff went on to arrange for film and television, founded Walton Music and created the Norman Luboff Choir, which became one of the most successful American choral ensembles of the mid-century. His radio years are therefore central to the story: they were where large-scale choral sound became both his profession and his public signature.

profiles.name: Jack Meakin
profiles.excerpt: Jack Meakin combined the jobs of pianist, arranger, producer, composer and orchestra leader, bringing a practical craftsman's approach to The Great Gildersleeve and other major radio programs.
profiles.bio_html:
Jack Meakin approached radio music as work to be built, tested and delivered on time. Born John Brunker Meakin, he began professionally as a pianist and arranger, working for NBC in San Francisco and arranging for Meredith Willson before moving into network production. A 1946 Radio Life profile emphasized how unusual his path was: he had produced programs including Chamber Music Society of Lower Basin Street, Hour of Charm, Kay Kyser's program, This Is War and The Telephone Hour before returning more fully to music.

Meakin became especially associated with The Great Gildersleeve, where his orchestra supported comedy without competing with it. He also composed and arranged themes and later worked with Groucho Marx. His own comments rejected the romantic idea that composers simply waited for inspiration; he described composition as disciplined labor, a particularly fitting philosophy for weekly broadcasting.

Golden Radio Hour's broader people index currently preserves 334 Great Gildersleeve composer, music and performer-tagged credits for Meakin. Those records document a sustained musical role across years of the series and belong with his work as a conductor and composer, not among acting credits.

profiles.name: Doc Whipple
profiles.excerpt: Clark 'Doc' Whipple was a radio organist whose instrument supplied the connective tissue and atmosphere for serials and mystery programs including The Mysterious Traveler.
profiles.bio_html:
Clark “Doc” Whipple belongs to the working tradition of radio organists whose names rarely appeared above the title even though their instruments were heard throughout the broadcast day. Organ music could establish location, bridge scenes, underline suspense and carry a serial through transitions without the expense or logistical weight of a full orchestra.

Surviving program records credit Whipple as organist on The Mysterious Traveler, including the 1944 broadcast “The Queen of the Cats.” Organ-history sources also associate him with daytime programs such as Ma Perkins and The Light of the World. GRH's detailed people data currently carries seven Mysterious Traveler organist credits, while the performer index separately associates him with John Steele, Adventurer.

The available historical record does not yet support a detailed personal-life biography for Whipple. GRH therefore keeps his page centered on the documented craft: a professional radio organist whose work supplied mood and continuity to programs where the music was essential even when the musician remained largely invisible.
